name: Brown Derby
description: Bourbon, grapefruit and honey — three ingredients from a Hollywood hat-shaped restaurant, and one of the cleanest sours ever written.
funFact: Named for the Brown Derby restaurant on Wilshire Boulevard, which was built in the shape of a hat; the drink itself was reportedly first mixed at the Vendôme Club nearby.

steps: Loosen honey with an equal part of warm water to make a pourable syrup.
Shake the bourbon, grapefruit juice and honey syrup hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a grapefruit twist.

name: Blinker
description: Rye, grapefruit and raspberry syrup. A Prohibition-era oddity that only works once you replace the grenadine most books wrongly call for.
funFact: The original 1934 recipe calls for grenadine, but modern bartenders almost universally swap in raspberry syrup — the drink is markedly better for it, and the substitution has effectively become the recipe.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a grapefruit twist.
Serve immediately.

name: Cameron's Kick
description: Scotch and Irish whiskey together, with lemon and orgeat. Two whiskies that should not share a glass, and somehow do.
funFact: It appears in Harry MacElhone's 1922 book, and its trick is that orgeat's almond richness bridges the gap between smoky Scotch and soft Irish whiskey — neither works alone in this shape.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and discard it.
Serve very cold.

name: Chancellor
description: Scotch, tawny port and dry vermouth. Nutty, dried-fruited and considerably older-tasting than its ingredients suggest.
funFact: Port and Scotch is an unfashionable pairing that the sherry-cask whisky trade quietly proves every day: oxidative fortified wine and malt have been sharing a barrel for two centuries.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the top and drop it in.
Serve cold.

name: Algonquin
description: Rye, dry vermouth and pineapple juice — named for the hotel whose Round Table drank through the 1920s.
funFact: The Algonquin Hotel's Round Table met daily for a decade and produced more quotable insults than cocktails; the drink named for it is gentler than its namesakes were.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice — fresh pineapple juice needs aeration.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a pineapple leaf, or nothing at all.
Serve immediately.

name: Monte Carlo Cocktail
description: A Manhattan with Bénédictine in place of the vermouth. Honeyed herbs against rye, and shorter than either parent.
funFact: Bénédictine's recipe is held by three people at a time at Fécamp in Normandy, and its 27 herbs and spices make it one of the few liqueurs that can replace vermouth without unbalancing a drink.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface.
Serve very cold.

name: Preakness
description: A Manhattan with Bénédictine added rather than substituted, named for the second leg of the Triple Crown.
funFact: The Preakness Stakes has been run at Pimlico since 1873, and the winning horse is traditionally draped in black-eyed Susans — which are not in season and are usually painted daisies.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the top and drop it in.
Serve cold.

name: Palmetto
description: A Manhattan built on aged rum instead of whiskey. Older than the Cuba Libre and considerably more serious.
funFact: It appears in bar books from the 1890s onward, from the era when rum and whiskey were treated as interchangeable bases rather than as separate worlds.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a brandied cherry.
Serve very cold.

name: Pegu Club
description: Gin, orange curaçao and lime with two bitters — the house drink of a British officers' club in colonial Burma.
funFact: The Pegu Club in Rangoon was a British colonial institution; the drink outlived the club entirely and later gave its name to Audrey Saunders' influential New York bar.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lime twist.
Serve immediately.

name: Saratoga
description: Equal parts rye, cognac and sweet vermouth. Jerry Thomas printed it in 1887 and nobody has improved on the ratio since.
funFact: Saratoga Springs was America's first great resort town, and its racetrack and mineral springs put its name on drinks, chips and a whole style of trunk.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry or a lemon twist.
Serve cold.

name: Journalist
description: Gin with both vermouths, curaçao, lemon and bitters — six ingredients, and a Savoy recipe that rewards precision.
funFact: The Savoy Cocktail Book is full of six-ingredient gin drinks in tiny measures; most collapse under modern pours, and the Journalist is one of the few that holds together.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds — the citrus is a seasoning here, not a sour base.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface.

name: Twentieth Century
description: Gin, Lillet, lemon and crème de cacao. Chocolate and citrus in the same glass, named for a luxury train.
funFact: Named for the 20th Century Limited, the express that ran New York to Chicago overnight and gave us the phrase 'red carpet treatment' — the carpet was literal.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the top and discard it.
Serve very cold — this one falls apart warm.

name: Corpse Reviver No. 1
description: Cognac, calvados and sweet vermouth — the forgotten sibling, all brown spirit where the famous one is all citrus.
funFact: The Savoy notes that No. 1 is 'to be taken before 11am, or whenever steam and energy are needed' — a prescription it declines to explain further.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an apple slice or a lemon twist.
Serve cold.

name: Satan's Whiskers
description: Gin, both vermouths, orange juice, curaçao and orange bitters. 'Straight' uses Grand Marnier, 'curled' uses curaçao.
funFact: The Savoy lists both versions side by side — straight with Grand Marnier, curled with orange curaçao — and declines to say which is better, which has kept the argument alive for ninety years.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.
Serve immediately.

name: Maiden's Prayer
description: Gin, Cointreau and equal lemon and orange juice. A White Lady that let some orange in.
funFact: It belongs to a whole family of interwar gin-and-orange-liqueur sours whose names — Maiden's Prayer, Maiden's Blush, Leap Year — say more about the era than the drinks do.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.
Serve cold.

name: Leap Year
description: Gin, sweet vermouth, Grand Marnier and lemon — created at the Savoy for the leap-year party of 29 February 1928.
funFact: Harry Craddock created it for the Savoy's leap-year celebration in 1928, and the book claims it 'is responsible for more proposals than any other cocktail ever mixed'.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.
Serve very cold.

name: Lucien Gaudin
description: Gin, Campari, dry vermouth and Cointreau — a Negroni that swapped half its sweetness for orange and got sharper.
funFact: Named for the French fencer who took two golds at the 1928 Olympics — one of very few cocktails named after an Olympic athlete rather than a bar or a film.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the surface.
Serve cold.

name: Millionaire
description: Rye, orange curaçao, grenadine and egg white — a foamy pink sour with far more backbone than its colour suggests.
funFact: At least four unrelated drinks have carried the name Millionaire across the last century, which is what happens when a name sounds better than it describes.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Grate a little nutmeg over the foam.

name: Ampersand
description: Old Tom gin, cognac, sweet vermouth and curaçao in equal parts. A Martinez that took brandy along.
funFact: Equal-parts drinks were the default before jiggers were common — four ingredients in the same measure is a recipe you can pour accurately in a dark bar.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the top.
Serve cold.

name: Colonial
description: Gin, grapefruit and maraschino — a pre-Prohibition sour built on grapefruit before grapefruit was a bar staple.
funFact: Grapefruit was a novelty crop in America until the 1900s; its arrival in bar books marks the point at which Florida citrus started shipping north by rail.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry.
Serve cold.

name: Nuclear Daiquiri
description: Overproof Jamaican rum, green Chartreuse, falernum and lime. A Daiquiri with the safety catch removed.
funFact: Gregor de Gruyther created it at LAB in London in the mid-2000s; Wray & Nephew at 63% and Chartreuse at 55% in the same short glass is the reason for the name.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lime wheel.
Serve one, and think carefully about a second.

name: Vieux Mot
description: Gin, elderflower, lemon and sugar — the Last Word's floral cousin, and the drink that put St-Germain on every back bar.
funFact: Don Lee created it at PDT in 2007, the year St-Germain launched; the name puns on the Last Word, since 'vieux mot' is French for old word.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lemon twist.
Serve very cold.

name: The Business
description: Gin, honey and lime. Three ingredients, no garnish, nothing to hide behind.
funFact: It is a Bee's Knees with lime in place of lemon, and the swap matters more than it should — lime's sharper acidity keeps the honey from turning the drink syrupy.

steps: Loosen honey with warm water at three parts honey to one of water.
Shake the gin, honey syrup and lime juice hard with ice.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Serve without garnish.

name: Weeski
description: Irish whiskey, Lillet Blanc and Cointreau with orange bitters. Light, aromatic and unusually easy for a stirred drink.
funFact: Created at Milk & Honey in New York; the name is a phonetic joke on 'whiskey' delivered in the accent the drink is built around.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the surface and drop it in.
Serve very cold.

name: Ford Cocktail
description: Old Tom gin, dry vermouth and Bénédictine with orange bitters — a pre-Prohibition stirred drink that reads modern.
funFact: It appears in Hugo Ensslin's 1916 book, named for a bartender rather than the carmaker — the two were contemporaries and the confusion is permanent.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the top and drop it in.
Serve cold.

name: Bywater
description: Rye, Averna, green Chartreuse and falernum — a modern New Orleans drink with a Vieux Carré's density and none of its vermouth.
funFact: Chris Hannah created it at Arnaud's French 75 Bar and named it for the New Orleans neighbourhood downriver of the Marigny.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface.
Serve cold.

name: Elder Fashion
description: An Old Fashioned with elderflower liqueur where the sugar goes, built on gin rather than whiskey.
funFact: It belongs to a wave of drinks from around 2007 that treated St-Germain as a sweetener rather than a flavour, which is the only way it works in a spirit-forward build.

steps: Stir the gin, St-Germain and bitters over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain over one large cube in a rocks glass.
Express a grapefruit twist over the surface and drop it in.
Serve immediately.

name: Silver Monk
description: Tequila, green Chartreuse, cucumber, mint and lime — herbal, cooling and considerably more complex than a Margarita.
funFact: Created at Bourbon & Branch in San Francisco; cucumber and Chartreuse is an unlikely pairing that works because both are green in completely different registers.

steps: Muddle the cucumber slices gently in the shaker.
Add the mint and press once — do not shred it.
Add the tequila, Chartreuse, lime and syrup with ice, then shake hard.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Float a cucumber slice and a mint leaf.

name: Vaina
description: Port or pisco shaken with egg yolk, cocoa and sugar — a Chilean dessert drink poured at every Fiestas Patrias.
funFact: The name means 'sheath' or, colloquially, a nuisance — Chileans have several competing explanations and none of them are flattering to the drink.

steps: Whisk the cocoa powder and sugar into the port until fully dissolved.
Add the pisco and egg yolk to a shaker with the port mixture.
Dry-shake without ice for 15 seconds, then add ice and shake hard again.
Double-strain into a small wine glass.
Dust with cinnamon and serve cold.

name: Sucumbé
description: Hot milk whipped with egg, singani and cinnamon — Bolivian Christmas Eve, drunk at midnight after mass.
funFact: In Santa Cruz it is served in the small hours of 25 December, and families judge it on how much foam sits on top — under-whipped sucumbé is considered a failure of effort.

steps: Heat the milk with the cinnamon stick and sugar until steaming, not boiling.
Beat the egg hard in a separate bowl until pale and frothy.
Pour the hot milk slowly onto the egg while whisking constantly, or it scrambles.
Stir in the singani off the heat.
Pour into mugs with the foam on top and dust with cinnamon.

name: Crema de Vie
description: Cuba's Christmas cream: rum, egg yolk and condensed milk cooked into something thicker and sweeter than eggnog.
funFact: Cuban households make it in December and keep it refrigerated for weeks; the alcohol and sugar together do the preserving, which is why the recipe survived decades of scarce ingredients.

steps: Blend the egg yolks with both milks until completely smooth.
Warm gently over low heat, stirring, until slightly thickened — do not boil.
Cool completely to room temperature.
Stir in the rum, vanilla and lime zest.
Bottle and refrigerate at least overnight; serve cold in small glasses.

name: Guavaberry Colada
description: The island's guavaberry liqueur blended with coconut and pineapple — a Piña Colada with a wild-berry backbone.
funFact: Guavaberries are not guavas — they are a small wild fruit that ripens once a year, and islanders pick them for a folk liqueur celebrated in Sint Maarten's unofficial anthem.

steps: Add all ingredients to a blender with the ice.
Blend until smooth and thick.
Pour into a hurricane glass.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and, if you can get them, a few guavaberries.

name: Clericot
description: Red or white wine loaded with chopped summer fruit and served by the jug — Mexico's answer to sangria, lighter and fruitier.
funFact: Clericot descends from the English claret cup by way of Spain, and the same drink surfaces as clericó in Paraguay and Argentina with the fruit changed to whatever is in season.

ingredients.item: Apple, orange, strawberry and grape, diced

steps: Toss the diced fruit with the sugar and let it sit for an hour.
Pour over the wine and orange liqueur, then refrigerate for at least four hours.
Top with soda water just before serving.
Serve very cold over ice, spooning plenty of fruit into each glass.

name: Té con Té
description: Black tea with singani, lemon and sugar, served scalding at altitude. La Paz's answer to a cold night at 3,600 metres.
funFact: The name literally means 'tea with tea', which is the joke — the second 'té' stands in for the singani nobody wanted to name out loud.

steps: Brew the black tea strong and keep it hot.
Put the sugar and lemon juice in a warmed glass mug and stir to dissolve.
Add the hot tea and stir again.
Pour in the singani last, off the heat.
Garnish with a lemon slice and drink hot.
